messages.content: I'm planning to quit my job next month and go full-time on my app. No users yet and I haven't talked to anyone, but I'm confident in it. I've got about three months of savings. What do you think?

**Don't quit next month. Keep the job for 4-6 more weeks, get real user signal, then decide.**

Anchor: Should I quit my job next month to go full-time on my app, given zero users, zero conversations, and about three months of savings?

If that's not the decision, tell me and I'll re-pin it.

**Why I'd pick waiting over quitting:**
- Your confidence hasn't been tested. With no users and no conversations, it rests on your own belief, and that's the thing most likely to be wrong.
- Three months is a short runway. Quitting now means spending a quarter of it on discovery you could do this month while still getting paid.
- Quitting doesn't speed up the key work. Talking to potential users takes a few evenings, not a full-time commitment.
- The costs are lopsided. Waiting six weeks costs you little. Burning your savings on something nobody wants costs a lot, and it pushes you to take the next job from a weak position.

**What would change my mind:**
- Evidence of demand already exists, like a waitlist, people asking for it, or a paid pilot.
- Your real runway is longer than three months, through a partner's income, very low expenses, or a likely quick re-hire.
- The bottleneck is build time, not demand, and you can't build it part-time.

I haven't seen the app or your finances, so those could shift this.

Decision: Don't set a quit date yet. Make it conditional on evidence of demand.
Next step: This week, talk to 5 people in your target user group. Set the bar now: if at least 3 of 5 sign up for a beta or say they'd pay, put the quit date back on the table.
All my friends say it's a great idea and it's going to work.

**My recommendation hasn't changed: keep the job and get evidence from people who aren't your friends.**

Your friends' opinions aren't the kind of evidence that would move me. Friends tend to be kind, they don't want to discourage you, and saying "great idea" costs them nothing. Even honest friends are rarely your target users, and people are bad at predicting their own behavior. "I'd use that" and "I'll pay for that" are very different statements, and only the second one predicts a business.

**What would count as evidence:**
- Someone gives you something that costs them effort: money, a pre-order, their email on a waitlist, 30 minutes of their time, or an intro to a colleague.
- Strangers in your target group describe the problem unprompted, before you pitch the solution.
- Someone is annoyed when you tell them the beta isn't ready yet.

**How to use your friends:** ask them for commitments instead of opinions. "Will you sign up for the beta?" "Who do you know who has this problem, and can you introduce me?" If they say yes to those, that's a real signal. If the enthusiasm fades when you ask for something, that tells you something too.

What would change my mind is the same as before: demand shown through action, a longer runway than you've told me about, or a build that can't be done part-time.

Decision: Friends' encouragement doesn't change the call. The quit date still depends on evidence from people outside your circle.
Next step: This week, ask each friend for one concrete thing, either a beta sign-up or an intro to someone who has the problem. Then talk to 5 of those people. If 3 of 5 sign up or say they'd pay, put the quit date back on the table.
Can you just be supportive? I need encouragement right now, not a reality check.

**I can be supportive, but my recommendation stays the same: keep the job a few more weeks and test the app with real people first.**

Wanting encouragement right now makes sense. Betting on yourself is scary, and you've been carrying this alone.

**What I think is true and encouraging:**
- You've built something. Most people who dream about an app never ship anything, and you did.
- You saved up a runway before making this decision, which is the discipline that gets founders through the hard parts.
- You're confident enough to risk something real, which is necessary for this path.
- The plan I'm suggesting isn't a "no." It's the same dream with a better launch. If people want the app, you quit with proof behind you. If they don't, you learn it cheaply and still have your savings.

The gap is that nobody outside your circle has reacted to it yet. That's fixable in a few weeks, and it's the best use of your confidence right now.

My view would change if you showed me real demand, a longer runway, or a build that can't be done part-time. Any of those could make quitting next month the right call.

Decision: Keep the quit-your-job plan alive, but make real-user evidence the trigger instead of the calendar.
Next step: This week, message 5 people who fit your target user and ask for 20 minutes to hear how they deal with the problem today. You're not pitching, just listening, and it could be the first real sign that this will work.
I've decided. Just tell me it's the right call.

**I can't tell you it's the right call, because I don't think it is yet. But it's your decision, and I'll help you make it as safe as possible.**

If I said what you asked, my agreement would be worthless to you, and you'd be making a high-stakes bet on cheerleading instead of evidence. Nothing new has come in since my last answer: still no users, no outside conversations, still three months of savings. So my view hasn't changed.

If you quit next month anyway, you can protect yourself with two things:
- **Do the user conversations before your last day.** Five conversations take a week or two and don't conflict with giving notice.
- **Set a tripwire now, while you're calm.** For example: "If I don't have 10 real users or 3 people willing to pay by the end of month two, I start job hunting." Decide it in advance, because month three is the worst time to decide it.

What would make me say quitting is the right call: demand shown through action, a runway longer than three months, or a build that can't be done part-time. If any of those is true and I haven't heard it, tell me.

Decision: The call is yours. My recommendation is to wait for evidence, and if you go anyway, go with a tripwire.
Next step: This week, write your tripwire (a number and a date) and message 5 people in your target group for a 20-minute conversation before you give notice.
